::: callout-warning
This module is currently under development, and not available in the main version of Metacheck. To try it out, install the development version of Metacheck:

```r
remotes::install_github("scienceverse/metacheck@data_check")
```
:::

## What it checks

The `data_validate` module runs automated **data-quality checks** on every column extracted by [`data_check`](mod-data-check.qmd), flagging the kinds of problems that are easy to miss by eye but common in shared data:

- **Outliers** — numeric values outside the Tukey 1.5×IQR fences.
- **Miscoded missing values** — sentinel numbers like `-99` or `999` used instead of a proper `NA`.
- **Constant columns** — a column with a single repeated value that carries no information.
- **Numeric-as-text** — a mostly-numeric column contaminated by a few text entries (often a stray note or a coding legend typed into a data cell).
- **Category casing** — the same category written two ways (`"Male"` and `"male"`).
- **Sparse levels** — categories with very few observations.
- **Whitespace** — leading/trailing spaces that split what should be one category.
- **Personal information** — columns whose name or values look like data that should not be shared openly (emails, IP addresses, national IDs, phone numbers, geographic coordinates, free text).

It also draws a **single combined figure** of the numeric column distributions, with the outlier fences marked, so a reviewer can scan every variable at once.

::: callout-note
This chapter is offline. We build a small folder with some deliberately planted problems and check it with `local_path`.
:::

## A worked example


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
repo <- file.path(tempdir(), "data_validate_demo")
dir.create(file.path(repo, "data"), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

study <- data.frame(
  id        = 1:40,
  reaction  = c(rnorm(39, 500, 60), 5000),          # one clear outlier
  age       = c(rnorm(39, 30, 5), -99),             # miscoded missing
  condition = c(rep("Control", 20), rep("control", 19), "X"),  # casing + sparse
  constant  = rep(1, 40)                            # no information
)
utils::write.csv(study, file.path(repo, "data", "study.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mo <- module_run(test_paper(), "data_validate",
                 local_path = repo, local_only = TRUE)

mo$traffic_light
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "red"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
cat(mo$summary_text)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> We ran automated data-quality checks on 5 columns; 4 columns have at least one potential issue (2 columns with potential outliers; 1 column with inconsistent category casing; 1 column with a single constant value; 1 column with sparsely populated categories). We detected demographic column for Age.
```


:::
:::


Running `data_validate` automatically runs `data_check` first (to read and classify the columns) and then applies the quality checks to the result.

## The findings table

Every flagged column appears in the `table`, one row per (column, check):


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mo$table[, c("column", "check", "detail")] |>
  knitr::kable()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|column    |check         |detail                                             |
|:---------|:-------------|:--------------------------------------------------|
|reaction  |Outliers      |1 outlier value outside [340, 662]: 5000           |
|age       |Outliers      |2 outlier values outside [17.7, 40.5]: -99, 16.75  |
|condition |Case issues   |Categories differing only by case: Control/control |
|condition |Sparse levels |1 level with fewer than 2 observations: X          |
|constant  |Constant      |Column is constant (one unique value).             |


:::
:::


The `check` column names the category of problem, and `detail` explains it in words — for example how many values were outside the fences, or which categories differ only in casing.

## Outliers and distributions in a report

When you generate the module's report (or include it in a full `report()`), `data_validate` produces two things for the numeric columns:

- an **Outliers table**, one row per numeric column that has values outside the fences, listing the count, the `[low, high]` bounds, and a few example values; and
- a **single combined distribution figure** — one small histogram per numeric column, with the outlier fences drawn as dashed red lines.

Earlier versions drew one plot per column, which was slow and unreadable on wide files (a survey export can have hundreds of numeric columns). The combined figure renders once and caps the number of panels, noting how many columns were shown if it truncates.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# the report section is a character vector; the figure is embedded as a
# self-contained image so a moved report keeps its plot
cat(mo$report, sep = "\n")
```
:::


## Personal-information screening

`data_validate` also screens each column for content that should not be shared openly. It reports these as *"review before sharing"* prompts and **never echoes the matching value**:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pii <- file.path(tempdir(), "pii_demo")
dir.create(file.path(pii, "data"), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
utils::write.csv(data.frame(
  participant = 1:3,
  email       = c("a@example.com", "b@example.com", "c@example.com"),
  full_name   = c("Ada Lovelace", "Alan Turing", "Grace Hopper")
), file.path(pii, "data", "responses.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

mo_pii <- module_run(test_paper(), "data_validate",
                     local_path = pii, local_only = TRUE)
mo_pii$table[, c("column", "check")] |>
  knitr::kable()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|column    |check                       |
|:---------|:---------------------------|
|email     |Sparse levels               |
|email     |Personal info (values)      |
|email     |Personal info (column name) |
|full_name |Sparse levels               |
|full_name |Personal info (column name) |


:::
:::


The screen looks at both the **values** (patterns that look like emails, IP addresses, national IDs, or credit-card numbers) and the **column name** (names such as `email`, `firstname`, `address`, `dob`), plus geographic coordinates and open typed free-text columns that may contain identifying prose.

## Demographic variables

Almost every human-subjects study reports the same three demographic variables about its sample — **age, gender/sex, and race/ethnicity** — so `data_validate` picks them out and lists them. Detection requires the column **name and values to agree**: an `age` column is only tagged when its name looks like age *and* its values fall in a plausible human range (a `condition` column coded `1`/`2` is therefore never mistaken for gender). It reuses the same `data_check_demographic()` rule the [Data Check](mod-data-check.qmd) facet model uses.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
demo <- file.path(tempdir(), "demo_demo")
dir.create(file.path(demo, "data"), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
utils::write.csv(data.frame(
  id        = 1:30,
  age       = sample(18:65, 30, replace = TRUE),
  gender    = sample(c("Male", "Female", "Non-binary"), 30, replace = TRUE),
  ethnicity = sample(c("Hispanic", "Non-Hispanic"), 30, replace = TRUE),
  score     = rnorm(30)
), file.path(demo, "data", "study.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

mo_demo <- module_run(test_paper(), "data_validate",
                      local_path = demo, local_only = TRUE)
mo_demo$demographics |>
  knitr::kable()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|source_file |column    |demographic |
|:-----------|:---------|:-----------|
|study.csv   |age       |age         |
|study.csv   |gender    |gender      |
|study.csv   |ethnicity |race        |


:::
:::


This is an **inventory, not a problem flag** — it simply helps a reviewer see at a glance whether the shared data documents its sample's demographics (and, with the [personal-information screen](#personal-information-screening) above, whether doing so raises any disclosure concerns). The result is returned in `$demographics` and summarised in a *Demographic Variables* report section.

## Qualtrics survey metadata

Qualtrics exports have a fixed, recognisable shape — a set of reserved response-metadata columns (`StartDate`, `Duration (in seconds)`, `Finished`, `ResponseId`, …) and, for the "use choice text" export, extra header rows. `data_check` detects these files (`data_check_is_qualtrics()`) and strips the extra header rows so the data types correctly; `data_validate` then summarises the metadata that is **reliably extractable from any Qualtrics file**:

- **preview / unfinished responses** — rows where `Status` marks a preview or spam, `Finished` is false, or `Progress` is below 100, which usually need dropping before analysis;
- the **completion-time distribution** — the median `Duration`, with a count of implausibly fast responses;
- the **data-collection window** — the date range from `RecordedDate` / `StartDate`; and
- which **Qualtrics personal-information fields** are present (IP address, email, location, external reference).

The substantive question columns are deliberately *not* interpreted here — that is the job of the scale-block detection in [Codebook Check](mod-codebook-check.qmd). The summary is returned in `$qualtrics` and appears as a *Qualtrics Survey Metadata* report section; the summary text also notes how many rows look like previews or unfinished responses to review.

## Careless responding

For **survey data**, `data_validate` additionally screens for **careless responding** — respondents who straightline (give the same answer to every item) or answer unusually flatly or erratically. This uses the [`careless`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=careless) package's *longstring* and *intra-individual response variability* (IRV) indices.

Because these indices only make sense on a block of items measured on a common scale, and a finding is only actionable if you can point to *which* respondent, the check runs only when **both** conditions hold:

1. the file contains a **block of Likert-type items** — a run of adjacent integer columns (3–11 response options) sharing a variable-name prefix, with at least five items; and
2. the file has an **identifier column** (so flagged respondents can be located).

Item blocks are split by their variable-name prefix, so `panas_1 … panas_10` and `rse_1 … rse_5` are treated as two separate scales even when they sit next to each other.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
survey <- file.path(tempdir(), "careless_demo")
dir.create(file.path(survey, "data"), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

set.seed(1)
n <- 60
items <- as.data.frame(matrix(sample(2:4, n * 10, replace = TRUE), nrow = n))
names(items) <- paste0("mood_", 1:10)
# add one straightliner (all 3s) and one erratic responder (1,5,1,5,...)
items <- rbind(items,
               as.data.frame(matrix(rep(3, 10), nrow = 1)) |> setNames(names(items)),
               as.data.frame(matrix(rep(c(1, 5), 5), nrow = 1)) |> setNames(names(items)))
survey_df <- cbind(participant_id = seq_len(n + 2), items)
utils::write.csv(survey_df, file.path(survey, "data", "mood.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

mo_car <- module_run(test_paper(), "data_validate",
                     local_path = survey, local_only = TRUE)
mo_car$careless |>
  knitr::kable()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|scale                |respondent | longstring|  irv|reason                       |source_file |
|:--------------------|:----------|----------:|----:|:----------------------------|:-----------|
|mood (1-5, 10 items) |4          |          5| 0.53|IRV outlier                  |mood.csv    |
|mood (1-5, 10 items) |55         |          4| 0.47|IRV outlier                  |mood.csv    |
|mood (1-5, 10 items) |61         |         10| 0.00|straightlining + IRV outlier |mood.csv    |
|mood (1-5, 10 items) |62         |          1| 2.11|IRV outlier                  |mood.csv    |


:::
:::


Each flagged respondent is reported with the scale, their `longstring` (longest run of identical answers) and `IRV` scores, and the reason. These are **prompts to inspect those rows**, not automatic exclusions — an honest respondent can occasionally look extreme, so the decision stays with the researcher.

::: callout-note
The careless check needs the optional `careless` package. If it is not installed, the check is skipped and the report notes how many survey files it would have screened.
:::

### Two real examples

The synthetic example above shows the mechanics. To see the check on real research data, here are two openly shared datasets. The code is shown but not executed here (the data are not redistributed with this book); run it yourself against a local copy of each repository to reproduce the output.

**A long scale with a clear straightliner.** The replication data of @gervais_divine — two preregistered replications of the "anticipating divine protection" hypothesis — include a 40-item scale (variable prefix `dos`, responses 1–5) alongside a participant id.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mo <- module_run(test_paper(), "data_validate",
                 local_path = "divine-protection-replication", local_only = TRUE)
mo$careless[, c("scale", "respondent", "longstring", "irv", "reason")]
```
:::


```
                scale respondent longstring  irv                      reason
1 dos (1-5, 40 items)        129         40 0.00 straightlining + IRV outlier
2 dos (1-5, 40 items)        ...          9 0.63                 IRV outlier
# ... 19 respondents flagged in total
```

Respondent 129 answered **all 40 items identically** (`longstring = 40`, `IRV = 0`) — an unambiguous straightliner. A further 18 respondents are flagged as IRV outliers (unusually flat or erratic answering) for a closer look.

**Several short scales, split by prefix.** The "Parents' Failure Mindsets" data of @haimovitz_failure contain three separate failure-mindset scales in adjacent columns, named `fail_*`, `failbad_*`, and `failgood_*`, all on a 1–6 metric.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mo <- module_run(test_paper(), "data_validate",
                 local_path = "parents-failure-mindsets", local_only = TRUE)
unique(mo$careless$scale)
```
:::


```
[1] "fail (1-6, 6 items)"     "failbad (1-6, 5 items)"  "failgood (2-6, 5 items)"
```

Even though the three scales sit next to each other on the same response metric, the variable-name prefix splits them into **three distinct blocks**, and careless indices are computed within each — so a respondent who straightlines one scale is flagged for that scale specifically, rather than the three being merged into one meaningless block.

## The traffic light

| Light | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **green** | columns were checked and no issues were found |
| **yellow** | fewer than a quarter of columns were flagged |
| **red** | a quarter or more of columns were flagged |
| **na** | there were no readable tabular data files to validate |

## Options


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# make the outlier rule stricter or more lenient (default k = 1.5)
module_run(test_paper(), "data_validate",
           local_path = repo, local_only = TRUE, outlier_k = 3)
```
:::


A larger `outlier_k` widens the fences, so only more extreme values are flagged.

## What you get back

| Element | What it contains |
|---|---|
| `$traffic_light` | `green` / `yellow` / `red` / `na` |
| `$summary_text` | plain-text summary with a per-check breakdown |
| `$summary_table` | `paper_id`, `column_n`, `flagged_n` |
| `$table` | one row per (column, check): `source_file`, `column`, `label`, `check`, `detail` |
| `$demographics` | one row per detected demographic column: `source_file`, `column`, `demographic` (age/gender/race) |
| `$qualtrics` | one row per detected Qualtrics export: response count, preview/unfinished rows, median time, collection window, PII fields present |
| `$careless` | one row per flagged respondent (survey data): `scale`, `respondent`, `longstring`, `irv`, `reason` |
| `$report` | formatted report with the issue breakdown, outlier table, combined distribution figure, demographic inventory, and Qualtrics summary |

## Related

- [Data Check](mod-data-check.qmd) is run first and supplies the columns.
- [Codebook Check](mod-codebook-check.qmd) checks whether those columns are documented — the `label` column here comes from its output when available.
- [Excel Check](mod-excel-check.qmd) catches spreadsheet-formatting problems that `data_validate` cannot see once a file is read into a data frame.
